{"id": "27:29/q17", "question": "What methodological claims about Qur'anic inimitability are reported alongside this verse?", "turns_on": "Bint questions the evidential basis for claims about lost books and the method used to discuss inimitability.", "positions": [{"id": "27:29/q17/p1", "position": "Inquiry should avoid speculative historical chains and contentious technical detours.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shati criticizes polemical proliferation and al-Rafi'i's conjectural method, including judgments about lost books and extravagant praise by supporters."}, {"id": "27:29/q17/p2", "position": "Al-Jahiz's lost book may have only begun establishing eloquence because rhetoric was not yet a discipline.", "reasons": "Al-Rafi'i conjectures this; Bint criticizes its speculative basis."}, {"id": "27:29/q17/p3", "position": "Al-Wasiti built on al-Jahiz, and Abd al-Qahir built Dalāʾil al-Iʿjāz on al-Wasiti.", "reasons": "Al-Rafi'i proposes this chain although the two earlier books are lost; Bint presents it among unsupported conjectures."}, {"id": "27:29/q17/p4", "position": "Ibn Suraqa's lost book cannot have been useful, since a useful book would have survived.", "reasons": "Al-Rafi'i infers this from non-survival; Bint identifies it as unsupported."}, {"id": "27:29/q17/p5", "position": "Al-Rafi'i first discussed inimitability within Tārīkh Ādāb al-ʿArab, then published that treatment separately for usefulness and accessibility.", "reasons": "Bint gives this publication history."}]}
{"id": "27:30/q01", "question": "What do the two pronouns in 'it is' refer to?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "27:30/q01/p1", "position": "The first refers to the letter; the second to its writing or contents.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Alusi distinguish the letter from its opening or unmentioned contents. Al-Baydawi allows the first to mean the letter or its heading, and the second its text or content. Al-Mawardi, al-Wahidi, al-Baghawi, al-Tabrisi and others explain that the queen identifies its sender and then its opening."}]}
{"id": "27:30/q02", "question": "Why are the two clauses introduced with emphatic inna?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "27:30/q02/p1", "position": "They answer implied questions about who sent the noble letter and what it contains.", "reasons": "Al-Kashshaf calls the second clause a resumption explaining the contents; al-Razi, al-Nasafi, Bursevi, al-Samin and al-Alusi identify the implied questions. Al-Alusi says the inferred questions warrant emphatic inna; al-Qurtubi allows an implied 'the speech' or a fresh sentence with the usual kasra."}]}
{"id": "27:30/q03", "question": "How are the two inna clauses read and grammatically construed?", "turns_on": "The transmitted kasra, fatha, conjunction and Ubayy variants require different links to the preceding 'letter' and different treatments of an; al-Samin weighs the grammatical analyses.", "positions": [{"id": "27:30/q03/p1", "position": "Both have kasra, making independent explanatory statements.", "reasons": "Al-Farra says both instances are read with kasra. Al-Qurtubi supplies an implicit 'the speech' or treats the second as a new sentence. Al-Samin says the common reading answers implied questions; Abu Hayyan says most readers use kasra."}, {"id": "27:30/q03/p2", "position": "Both hamzas have fatha, with the clauses appositional to 'letter.'", "reasons": "Ibn Abi Abla and Ikrima transmit the reading. Al-Farra and al-Nahhas permit apposition; al-Razi and al-Baydawi explain substitution for kitab. Al-Samin calls substitution, by inclusion or full substitution, the strongest analysis; Makki reports al-Farra allowed the form in speech, and al-Samin notes it is also transmitted as a reading."}, {"id": "27:30/q03/p3", "position": "Both hamzas have fatha because an omitted preposition or causal lam explains the letter's nobility.", "reasons": "Al-Farra and al-Nahhas describe accusative after an omitted preposition; al-Kashshaf, al-Razi, al-Baydawi, Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi connect the clauses to the reason the letter is noble. Al-Samin attributes the omitted causal lam to al-Zamakhshari."}, {"id": "27:30/q03/p4", "position": "The open clauses are governed as a predicate of karim.", "reasons": "Abu al-Baqa proposes this, but al-Samin finds it weak."}, {"id": "27:30/q03/p5", "position": "A reading adds a coordinating waw before the clause identifying Solomon.", "reasons": "Attributed to Abd Allah. Al-Kashshaf, Ibn Atiyya, al-Razi and al-Samin link it to the queen's previous statement that she received a letter. Al-Alusi records Abu Hayyan's coordination with 27:29 and another circumstantial parsing. Al-Qurtubi mentions the variant; Abu Hayyan describes a conjunction before the second clause."}, {"id": "27:30/q03/p6", "position": "Ubayy reads an with open hamza and quiescent nun before Solomon and the basmala, primarily as an explanatory particle.", "reasons": "Al-Farra cites wa-an before the basmala and says the opened particle joined to a clause can be lightened; he connects it with the following an la ta'lu and compares repeated an with 23:35. Ibn Atiyya specifies omission of ha. Al-Samin rejects the omitted-subject version under Basran rules: the subject must be the pronoun of circumstance, explained by a complete clause."}]}
{"id": "27:30/q04", "question": "What does 'from Solomon' express?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "27:30/q04/p1", "position": "Min marks the letter's origin, with a person standing for its place of origin.", "reasons": "Al-Burhan says min normally marks the beginning of an extent when paired with ila, literally or in sense; here Solomon stands for the source place."}]}
{"id": "27:30/q05", "question": "What inward meaning is given to Solomon's name?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "27:30/q05/p1", "position": "It points to the Essence granting preparedness and the faculties that actualize intellect and moral perfection.", "reasons": "Al-Qashani associates the name with potential made actual and fitting perfection in qualities and attributes."}]}
{"id": "27:30/q06", "question": "Did Solomon put his name before God's name in the actual letter?", "turns_on": "Whether the queen reproduced the physical order, summarized it, or distinguished a heading from its body; Abu Hayyan proposes protection of God's name, which al-Alusi disputes.", "positions": [{"id": "27:30/q06/p1", "position": "The letter itself began by naming Solomon and then gave the basmala.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya allows an eloquent sequence of address, divine name and demand. Abu Hayyan favors the apparent order and suggests protecting God's name from a disrespectful response by the unbelieving queen. Al-Biqai says this order does not detract from praise and can favor acceptance because people recognize truth through people. Al-Alusi reports a heading with Solomon's name. Al-Alusi rejects Abu Hayyan's protective explanation."}, {"id": "27:30/q06/p2", "position": "The basmala came first; the queen named the sender before quoting or summarizing the letter.", "reasons": "Al-Razi says Solomon opened with the basmala, while the order belongs to her report. Abu Hayyan transmits this alternative. Yazid ibn Ruman's transmitted letter begins with the basmala, then names Solomon and addresses Bilqis daughter of Dhi Sharh and her people. Al-Alusi says a signature after the basmala could have supplied his identity."}, {"id": "27:30/q06/p3", "position": "Solomon's name was an outer heading; the basmala began the written body.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan gives this alternative, and al-Alusi reports a view treating the first clause as the heading."}, {"id": "27:30/q06/p4", "position": "The queen summarized the sender and opening, so her order does not settle the original order.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya allows summary instead of exact sequence; Islahi says she did not read the whole letter aloud and notes ancient royal letters named sender and recipient. Tabatabai treats the message as meaning rather than verbatim wording."}]}
{"id": "27:30/q07", "question": "In letters, should the sender or recipient be named first?", "turns_on": "Prophetic and companion precedent for naming the sender first versus later communal custom allowing or favoring the recipient first.", "positions": [{"id": "27:30/q07/p1", "position": "Name the sender first.", "reasons": "Ibn Sirin reports the Prophet contrasting Persian practice of beginning with leaders and instructing a man to begin with himself. Anas says the Companions began letters to the Prophet with their own names despite his greater honor. Ibn al-Arabi says this was earlier messengers' custom. Al-Alusi notes that early letters named sender and recipient without a following prayer."}, {"id": "27:30/q07/p2", "position": "Naming the recipient first is also permissible, and may be preferable under prevailing custom.", "reasons": "Abu al-Layth appeals to communal consensus and practice; al-Qurtubi reports that in his time this was preferable except when addressing a servant or child. Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi transmit the permissive view."}]}
{"id": "27:30/q08", "question": "What is implicit in 'in the name of God'?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "27:30/q08/p1", "position": "An unstated clause supplies the action, such as 'this is in God's name' or 'in God's name at the start of everything.'", "reasons": "Abu Ubayda in Majaz gives both examples of the understood wording."}]}

{"id": "27:30/q10", "question": "What does the basmala say about God and His mercy?", "turns_on": "The notes draw different theological implications from God's name and the two mercy attributes.", "positions": [{"id": "27:30/q10/p1", "position": "It names the worship-worthy God and His encompassing majesty and generosity, with special mercy to whom He wills.", "reasons": "Al-Biqai says the divine name establishes Solomon's prophethood and describes general majesty and particular gifts. Al-Razi says the formula gives the knowledge needed before action and establishes God as existent, knowing, powerful, living, willing, wise and merciful."}, {"id": "27:30/q10/p2", "position": "Al-Rahman denotes mercy to all in this world and the next, and al-Rahim special mercy in the next.", "reasons": "Bursevi gives this distinction in his esoteric exposition."}, {"id": "27:30/q10/p3", "position": "Even idolaters acknowledge God's supreme lordship, so the divine name and attributes ennoble the letter.", "reasons": "Tabatabai says Sabian sun worshippers honor God as Lord of lords and understand His attributes as absence of ignorance, incapacity, death and cruelty."}]}
{"id": "27:30/q11", "question": "What inward meanings are read in the letters of the basmala?", "turns_on": "These are distinct letter-symbol readings reported by Bursevi.", "positions": [{"id": "27:30/q11/p1", "position": "Its letters signify divine permanence, splendor, sovereignty, oneness, beauty, majesty and identity.", "reasons": "Bursevi assigns ba to permanence, sin to splendor, mim to sovereignty, alif to oneness, the two lams to beauty and majesty, and ha to divine identity."}, {"id": "27:30/q11/p2", "position": "The opening ba suffices because all existence is covered by God's general or particular mercy.", "reasons": "Bursevi transmits this from some great Sufis."}, {"id": "27:30/q11/p3", "position": "Its nineteen letters send grace over seventeen thousand worlds.", "reasons": "Bursevi quotes Jami's Persian couplet with those numbers."}]}
{"id": "27:30/q12", "question": "What makes this letter 'noble'?", "turns_on": "The stated grounds are God's name, Solomon's authority together with it, God's precedence in the formula, or the seal.", "positions": [{"id": "27:30/q12/p1", "position": "Its divine opening gives it nobility.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayri reports this and applies it to prayer: prayer is noble with the naming formula and deficient without it. Ibn Atiyya cites a Prophetic report that speech without the basmala is deficient. Tabatabai says even idolaters acknowledge God's lordship and the letter's association with God raises its standing. Tabatabai explicitly invokes Bilqis's knowledge of Solomon's authority and the opening, citing 27:42."}, {"id": "27:30/q12/p3", "position": "Its nobility comes from naming God first instead of starting with the sender-and-recipient formula.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayri reports this separate explanation."}, {"id": "27:30/q12/p4", "position": "A letter's seal completes and ennobles it.", "reasons": "Al-Qurtubi cites a hadith calling the seal a letter's nobility; Ibn al-Muqaffa says an unsealed letter disrespects a brother, and Umar calls one unfinished or exposed. Solomon's letter was reportedly sealed with his signet."}]}
{"id": "27:30/q13", "question": "Was Solomon the first to write the full basmala?", "turns_on": "Whether the reported first use concerns the formula itself or only the Arabic wording and order of a translated original.", "positions": [{"id": "27:30/q13/p1", "position": "No one before Solomon wrote the full formula; it was unfamiliar to the queen and her people.", "reasons": "Qatada says earlier writing used 'In Your name, O Allah.' {"id": "27:30/q14", "question": "How did the Prophet's written invocation develop?", "turns_on": "The chronology of the basmala's revelation relative to this verse and whether intermediate written forms are counted.", "positions": [{"id": "27:30/q14/p1", "position": "It progressed in stages from 'In Your name, O God' through forms associated with 11:41 and 17:110 to the full basmala at this verse.", "reasons": "Al-Sha'bi supplies this sequence in Abd al-Razzaq, al-Mawardi, al-Durr and al-Alusi; the report in Ibn Abi Hatim says Arabs questioned al-Rahman and 17:110 permitted either divine name. Al-Mawardi calls the full formula the third written form. Islahi says the queen's emphasis illuminates this history."}, {"id": "27:30/q14/p2", "position": "He continued writing 'In Your name, O God' until this verse, then used the full basmala.", "reasons": "Maymun ibn Mihran, Abu Malik and Qatada transmit this shorter chronology. Al-Alusi notes Abu Dawud's mursal report from Abu Malik and parallel accounts. Ibn Kathir relays Maymun; al-Alusi says subsequent use of the full basmala became established."}, {"id": "27:30/q14/p3", "position": "Opening letters with the basmala fits its earlier revelation as the opening of God's Book, so a late adoption chronology is implausible.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi invokes its prior revelation and 1:1, says the reported late chronology is nearly impossible, and affirms that its earlier revelation should stand. He also says opening with the full formula after this verse became the Prophet's settled practice."}]}
{"id": "27:30/q15", "question": "Was the basmala itself the first revelation?", "turns_on": "Whether the basmala accompanying the first sura is counted as a separate first-revelation candidate.", "positions": [{"id": "27:30/q15/p1", "position": "It was first in an absolute sense because every sura's revelation includes its basmala.", "reasons": "Al-Suyuti argues it need not be a separate first-revelation opinion; al-Alusi accepts this conclusion, citing 1:1."}, {"id": "27:30/q15/p2", "position": "The soundest named first-revelation view is 96:1, with alternatives naming 74:1, al-Fatiha or the basmala.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi reports al-Suyuti's list; the distinction of basmala as a separate view is qualified by al-Suyuti's argument."}]}
{"id": "27:30/q16", "question": "How should the basmala be laid out and followed in written correspondence?", "turns_on": "The noted difference is early epistolary practice versus later scribal recommendations.", "positions": [{"id": "27:30/q16/p1", "position": "Put it on its own line and align the following prayer carefully.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi reports some eminent scholars' recommendation and al-Suli's manual: start at the page margin, align the prayer, avoid a short spill beyond the basmala, and do not center it."}, {"id": "27:30/q16/p2", "position": "Early letters did not add a prayer after the basmala; they simply named the sender and recipient.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi distinguishes early practice from the later layout with a following prayer."}]}
{"id": "27:30/q17", "question": "Is this basmala a complete verse, and how does it relate to other sura basmalas?", "turns_on": "The notes address different aspects of the formula's placement and verse status.", "positions": [{"id": "27:30/q17/p1", "position": "Here it is not a complete verse as the basmala in Hud is; the basmalas opening suras are separate verses revealed 114 times.", "reasons": "Bursevi compares 11:41 and counts one opening basmala for each sura."}, {"id": "27:30/q17/p2", "position": "This is the Qur'an's sole repetition of the full basmala inside a sura.", "reasons": "The Study Quran states the uniqueness of its placement."}]}

{"id": "27:30/q23", "question": "How was the letter delivered and found?", "turns_on": "The reports differ on the exact place and manner of the hoopoe's delivery.", "positions": [{"id": "27:30/q23/p1", "position": "The hoopoe dropped it through the queen's sun or palace window despite locked doors.", "reasons": "Wahb says it carried the letter in its leg and dropped it through the sun window. {"id": "27:30/q24", "question": "What did the letter demand of the queen and her people?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "27:30/q24/p1", "position": "They should not oppose, defy, refuse or disobey Solomon, and should come to him submitting.", "reasons": "Yahya, Qatada, al-Suddi, Sufyan and Zuhayr give the near-synonymous glosses; Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd says refusal would bring war and also accepts the literal arrogance sense. {"id": "27:30/q26", "question": "Why is Solomon's letter so brief, and what does its brevity show?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "27:30/q26/p1", "position": "It exemplifies prophetic and especially Solomonic eloquence: a few clear words give the necessary knowledge and command.", "reasons": "Yahya, Qatada and al-Mawardi describe prophetic letters as concise. {"id": "27:30/q28", "question": "Must a recipient answer a letter containing a greeting?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "27:30/q28/p1", "position": "Yes; an absent sender's written greeting is like a present person's greeting, so answering is required.", "reasons": "Al-Qurtubi draws the analogy and reports Ibn Abbas treating the reply as obligatory."}]}

{"id": "27:30/q30", "question": "What does this letter contribute to the sura's account of Solomon and Sheba?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "27:30/q30/p1", "position": "Its basmala and summons make the invitation both religious and political, leading into the queen's embrace of faith in the one God.", "reasons": "Kuranyolu links the letter to Solomon testing the hoopoe's news and asking for the queen's reply; Study Quran describes the encounter's endpoint as her faith."}]}
{"id": "27:35/q01", "question": "Why did the queen decide to send a gift?", "turns_on": "Whether the gift is chiefly appeasement, a test of kingship and prophecy, or a means to obtain information; these purposes often coexist.", "positions": [{"id": "27:35/q01/p1", "position": "She sought to conciliate Solomon, avert war or loss of her kingdom, and test whether he was a worldly king or a prophet.", "reasons": "Muqātil and al-Wāḥidī say she hoped wealth would appease him over her kingdom. Ṭabarī, Thaʿlabī, Baghawī, Qurṭubī, and others explain that a king would accept and withdraw or could be fought; a prophet would refuse and demand religious submission.
